sections.title: People & Politics
sections.description: Important developments in governments, societies and the people shaping the world.

cards.title: US Army delays Iowa explosive detonation amid legal challenges
cards.content: President Donald Trump has ordered the US Army to hold off on detonating five tons of toxic explosives in Iowa until a federal court and the state's incoming governor agree. The planned detonation, which was scheduled to take place at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, has faced legal challenges and public outcry over potential health and environmental hazards. The explosives, known as lead azide, are considered highly volatile and could pose serious health risks to humans and animals, particularly children. The US Army had planned to detonate the explosives on Wednesday, citing optimal weather conditions and safety measures. However, the plans are now on hold pending a court ruling and approval from the incoming governor. The Environmental Protection Agency has granted an emergency permit for the detonation, citing an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment. Local authorities, including the mayor of Middletown, have backed the detonation, saying it is necessary to ensure public safety.

cards.title: UK Sanctions Myanmar Military Leaders Over Rohingya Genocide
cards.content: The UK has sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in 2017. The ruling led to thousands of deaths and the forced displacement of over 700,000 Rohingya. The sanctions are joined by several other countries, including Australia, Belgium, Portugal, Spain, and Canada. The UK Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, urged Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and prevent such atrocities from happening again. He also called for an immediate pause in hostilities, the release of political prisoners, and dialogue towards an inclusive political settlement. The UK will raise the issue at the UN Security Council and pass new legislation to stop the supply of aviation fuel to the country.

cards.title: Turkish millionaire accuses adviser of £38m misappropriation
cards.content: Nebahat Isbilen, a Turkish millionaire, has accused her former business adviser Selman Turk of misappropriating £38m of her assets, including a £750,000 payment to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019. Isbilen claims she was misled about the payment's purpose, believing it was for help with her passport, when in reality it was intended to help her husband, a politician in prison in Turkey. Mountbatten-Windsor has repaid the payment and is expected to give evidence in December. Isbilen's lawyers say Turk deliberately and systematically abused her trust, transferring the money to companies he owned or controlled. The trial is ongoing, with a written judgment expected at a later date.

sections.title: Science and technology
sections.description: Discover breakthroughs in science, space, computing and emerging technology.

cards.title: Study Finds Genetic Links to Personality Traits in 1 Million People
cards.content: Researchers at the University of Tartu have discovered genetic connections that may influence human personality traits, such as being outgoing, organized, or worrisome. The study, which involved over one million people, found that nearly 1,000 genetic variants are associated with five major personality dimensions. The findings suggest that about 4.8% to 9.3% of personality differences can be attributed to genetics, with the remaining portion influenced by social relationships, environmental factors, and personal experiences. The study also found that people's self-reported personality traits are largely consistent with how others perceive them, and that personality traits can influence physical health, such as body weight, smoking, and alcohol consumption. The researchers emphasized that their findings do not establish cause and effect, and that further studies are needed to determine the relationship between personality and health.

cards.title: Diamond Amplifier Boosts Microwave Signals 1,000 Times for Quantum Computing
cards.content: Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology have developed a new amplifier that can strengthen microwave signals more than 1,000 times while adding very little noise, using an unlikely material: diamond. This amplifier, known as a diamond maser, can handle stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, potentially overcoming limitations that make today's quantum computers difficult to scale up. The findings were published in Nature Communications. This technology can be particularly useful for quantum computers that rely on spin-based qubits and has potential applications beyond quantum computing, such as spectroscopy and nuclear magnetic resonance.

cards.title: Estonian Tech Billionaire Jaan Tallinn to Gain Billions in Anthropic IPO
cards.content: Jaan Tallinn, an Estonian tech billionaire and AI safety advocate, is set to be one of the biggest winners in Anthropic's upcoming IPO, with his initial investment potentially returning tens of billions. Tallinn co-founded Skype and led Anthropic's first funding round, five years ago, before the company's Claude chatbot became a market success. Anthropic's IPO, set to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT, is expected to be the largest in history, valuing the company at around $1.4 trillion. Tallinn's exact return will depend on the level of dilution in subsequent funding rounds and whether he sold any shares. Despite his concerns about AI's existential risk, Tallinn's investment in Anthropic has paid off, and he will benefit from the company's commercial success, which some worry may come at the expense of AI safety.

sections.title: Health & wellness
sections.description: Medical research, public health and discoveries that affect everyday wellbeing.

cards.title: Frequent Short Walks Boost Blood Sugar Control, Study Shows
cards.content: Scientists have discovered that taking frequent short walks throughout the day can improve blood sugar control, particularly for people at risk of type 2 diabetes. In a study, participants were assigned to either walk for 45 minutes once a day or in 5-minute breaks throughout the day. The group that took frequent breaks saw a significant increase in time spent within a target blood sugar range, from 82% to 94%, whereas the group that walked in one continuous session experienced a decline. The study suggests that distributing physical activity throughout the day may be as important as the total amount of exercise, and that interrupting prolonged sitting with short walks may offer additional benefits for glucose regulation.

cards.title: CP research challenges previous findings, suggests complex condition
cards.content: New research on cerebral palsy (CP) challenges previous findings and proposes a different understanding of the condition. The study, published in the American Journal of Human Genetics, found that only 89 out of 515 previously linked genes showed a statistically significant association with CP. The researchers suggest that CP may not be a single disease, but rather a collection of symptoms arising from multiple underlying conditions. They propose a 'phenotypic paradigm' for understanding CP, considering it a clinical characteristic that can emerge from different genetic disorders and environmental influences. The study's findings do not disprove connections between CP and other genes, but rather highlight the need for further research and validation before these findings can be applied to patient care.

sections.title: Environment
sections.description: Climate, oceans, ecosystems and the changing planet around us.

cards.title: Global Treaty Proposed to Protect Soil, Citing Risk to $44 Trillion Annual Output
cards.content: Scientists argue that protecting soil requires countries to look beyond their borders, as the thin layer of soil covering Earth's surface is crucial for nourishing ecosystems, filtering water, and supporting life. Despite its importance, soil lacks a dedicated international treaty, with estimates suggesting up to 40 percent of the world's land is already degraded, putting $44 trillion in annual economic output at risk. A proposal for international protection is taking shape, with the University of Sydney's Aroura think tank outlining an eight-stage pathway towards a Global Convention to Secure Soil, targeting adoption in 2032. The authors argue that soil security cannot be achieved by countries acting independently, and that international cooperation is needed to match the scale of the problem, citing the example of ocean governance.

cards.title: Human metabolism's carbon dioxide emissions rise 74% in 30 years
cards.content: A new study by the University of Bath has found that the amount of carbon dioxide produced by human metabolism has increased by 74% over the past three decades, with the global total reaching an estimated 2.05 billion metric tons annually by 2015. The study, published in The Lancet Planetary Health, analyzed thousands of real-world measurements of CO2 production in people of all ages and found that the increase is mainly due to population growth, with more than 60% of the rise attributed to an increase in the number of people rather than a significant change in the amount produced by each individual. The researchers suggest that accounting for this activity could help scientists more accurately predict how effective carbon reduction strategies may be.

cards.title: Srinagar's Water Crisis Worsens due to Climate Change
cards.content: In Srinagar, a water crisis has been ongoing for years, causing daily struggles for residents like Mehak and Zamrood. The absence of a regular water supply has led to the installation of tanks and a hand pump at their homes. Climate change is affecting Doodh Ganga, a vital source of drinking water, causing erratic water supply, low flow, and dry taps. The river's water availability is decreasing due to rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and declining snowmelt. The Kashmir Valley's 24 watersheds, including Doodh Ganga, are experiencing similar impacts.

cards.title: Don Toliver Postpones London Shows After Manchester Concert Evacuated Over Unknown Substance
cards.content: US rapper Don Toliver has postponed two London shows after his Manchester concert was evacuated due to an unknown substance released into the crowd. The incident occurred on Sunday, leaving one person in hospital and 89 others showing symptoms believed to be linked to the exposure. Toliver's Wembley Arena show was rescheduled to December 14, while his O2 show was moved to December 15. The substance, which police initially believed to be tear gas, caused distressing scenes with people choking, screaming, and coughing up blood. The investigation into the incident is ongoing, with police testing items at the venue to identify the substance.

cards.title: Rugby's Christmas Gran Releases Charity Single for Crisis
cards.content: MJ, a 70-year-old woman from Rugby, is releasing a high-energy Christmas charity single called 'Christmas Day Is Coming'. The song, which she records as 'Christmas Gran', is a techno track meant to be danced and raved to, rather than a traditional Christmas song. MJ aims to raise money for the national charity Crisis, which helps people experiencing homelessness. She hopes to raise funds to support those who are 'lonely, lost, and on the streets in the cold throughout the winter'. MJ has collaborated with producer Andy Kulesza, who also praises her positive attitude and sense of humor, despite facing significant loss in her life. In the future, MJ plans to release a rap song, possibly featuring Stormzy.

sections.title: economy
sections.description: Markets, businesses, trade and economic changes shaping the global economy.

cards.title: Capita shares drop 70% as CEO quits amid UK pension scheme issues
cards.content: Shares in outsourcing company Capita have dropped by 70% after its CEO, Adolfo Hernandez, resigned amid ongoing issues with the UK's Civil Service pension scheme. The scheme, which manages pensions for 1.7 million public sector workers, has been plagued by delays in payments and controversy. Capita took over the scheme's administration in December, but has struggled to improve the situation. The company has revised its profit forecast downward, citing the pension scheme's problems and the loss of two major contracts. To address these issues, Capita plans to raise £190m through an equity offering. The saga has caused significant hardship for some pension scheme members, with some experiencing long delays in receiving payments, including bereavement payments. The Public Accounts Committee has been investigating the matter and is urging the new acting CEO, Pablo Andres, to take immediate action to resolve the issues.

cards.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Reinstated
cards.content: Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, has made a shocking return to the chipmaker after admitting to an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. The US government assured there were no national security concerns with his reinstatement, and President Trump revealed he had spoken directly to the Nvidia board. This U-turn comes after the board initially stated Huang would not be returning and the company was considering a shift in strategy. Huang's influence over Nvidia's pipeline of advanced microchips, crucial for the development of frontier artificial intelligence systems, has raised concerns about the future of the AI boom, the US tech stock market, and the global economy.

cards.title: Compass Group shifts UK listing to US stock market
cards.content: Catering giant Compass Group is planning to shift its primary stock market listing from the UK to the US, a move that will impact the London Stock Exchange. According to a source close to the company, the official announcement is expected to be made in the company's full-year results on Tuesday. Compass Group operates several brands that provide food and drink services to various places, such as football stadiums, universities, and corporations. The company's decision to list its shares on the US market is reportedly due to the growing number of investors and increasing business it has across the Atlantic, with North America accounting for two-thirds of its business. The move would follow several other UK-based companies that have left the UK to list their shares in the US, including tech firm Arm Holdings and pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca. The decision is expected to have no impact on the number of UK employees and Compass Group will likely retain a secondary listing in London.
